items.text: Keep Sikkim clean by using designated dustbins.
Carry reusable water bottles and shopping bags whenever possible.
Protect forests, alpine meadows, rivers, waterfalls and lakes.
Stay only on designated trekking trails and tourist routes.
Report forest fires, landslides or environmental hazards to local authorities.
Leave every destination cleaner than you found it.
Support eco-friendly tourism initiatives and sustainable travel practices.
Do not feed wild animals or birds.
Never disturb wildlife or their habitats.
Do not collect plants, flowers, medicinal herbs or rare species.
Avoid loud music inside forests and protected areas.
Never purchase products made from endangered wildlife.
Carry your waste back whenever bins are unavailable.
Separate biodegradable and plastic waste wherever facilities exist.
Use refillable bottles instead of disposable plastics.
Throw garbage into rivers, lakes or valleys.
Burn plastic or other waste.
Leave food wrappers along trekking routes.
Plastic carry bags
Plastic cups and plates
Disposable cutlery
Certain PET bottles and other banned plastic products
Carry a valid government-issued photo ID.
Keep digital and printed copies of permits.
Follow all instructions issued by permit authorities.
Travel only to destinations covered by your permit.
Hire only registered travel agencies and licensed taxi operators.
Follow speed limits on mountain roads.
Wear seat belts at all times.
Wear helmets while riding motorcycles.
Avoid driving during heavy rainfall, snowfall or landslides unless advised safe.
Follow police and traffic advisories.
Avoid excessive alcohol.
Ascend gradually whenever possible.
Rest if you experience altitude sickness.
Follow medical advice immediately if symptoms worsen.
Carry prescribed medicines if required.
Remove footwear where required.
Maintain silence inside monasteries.
Ask permission before photographing monks, ceremonies or local residents.
Respect prayer flags, prayer wheels and sacred monuments.
Walk clockwise around stupas and religious structures where customary.
Consider making voluntary donations only through authorised donation boxes.
Ask permission before photographing individuals.
Respect photography restrictions in religious and military areas.
Never fly drones in restricted or protected zones without official approval.
Avoid disturbing wildlife for photographs.
Choose authorised operators.
Wear certified safety equipment.
Follow guide instructions.
Inform someone about your itinerary.
Check weather conditions before departure.
Smoking near monasteries, temples and sacred places.
Consuming alcohol in religious or culturally sensitive locations.
Littering cigarette butts.
Drinking and driving under any circumstances.
Follow directions issued by Police, Tourism Officials, Forest Officials and Disaster Management Authorities.
Cooperate during landslides, road closures or weather-related restrictions.
Do not cross road barricades or restricted areas.
Buying authentic local handicrafts.
Staying in registered hotels and homestays.
Respecting local traditions and festivals.
Supporting local guides and businesses.
Avoiding bargaining that may unfairly impact small vendors.

intro: For domestic and foreign tourists visiting the protected areas of Sikkim — issued by the Tourism & Civil Aviation Department, Police Check Posts and authorised offices through registered Travel Agencies.
Protected Area Permits are issued to domestic tourists and locals for the protected areas across Sikkim.
Foreign tourists are permitted for Tsomgo Lake in East Sikkim and the Lachen–Lachung–Yumthang–Thangu Valley in North Sikkim.
Motorbikes must have an engine capacity of 150 cc or higher to be permitted entry into PAP areas.
Protected Area Permits for various destinations across Sikkim, grouped by district.

intro: Every foreigner (excluding people of Bhutanese origin) who wishes to enter and stay in a Protected or Restricted Area of Sikkim must obtain a Restricted Area Permit, issued free of cost by authorised offices of the Government of India and the Tourism Department.
Every foreigner (excluding people of Bhutanese origin) must fill the prescribed format provided at the permit office, attach the required documents, and seek approval from the competent authority.
Citizens of Nepal or Bangladesh may produce a valid identity card reflecting their origin while applying for the permit.
All foreigners visiting the State must register themselves within 24 hours of their arrival.
The Restricted Area Permit (RAP) is issued free of cost from the authorised offices listed below.
The issuance of a RAP requires prior clearance from the Ministry of Home Affairs in the following cases before applying.

Nationals, OCIs or citizens of Pakistan, Afghanistan or China — under the Prior Reference Category (PRC), including Hong Kong and Macau — must obtain prior approval from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, New Delhi before applying for a RAP.

Individuals of Pakistani, Afghan or Chinese origin (by birth), also under PRC including Hong Kong and Macau, must receive prior approval from the Ministry of Home Affairs, New Delhi before applying for a RAP.

Individuals born in, or who are nationals, OCIs or citizens of Myanmar or Nigeria, need prior clearance from either the Ministry of Home Affairs or the Home Department of Sikkim before entering the State.
On issue of the permit, a foreigner is allowed to visit the following places strictly for tourism purposes only.

Visiting Tsomgo Lake (East) or the Lachen–Lachung–Yumthang–Thangu Valley (North) needs a Protected Area Permit (PAP). Tsomgo Lake is a day excursion; North Sikkim valleys are issued for a minimum of 3 days / 2 nights up to a maximum of 5 days / 4 nights, supervised by a registered guide.
Foreigners are allowed to stay for a maximum duration of 30 days on issue of the permit.
Any extension of the permit period must be applied for at least 2 days before its expiry.
Extensions beyond 30 days are granted by the Foreigners Registration Office, Gangtok and the Superintendent of Police at Namchi, Mangan and Gyalshing — total stay must not exceed 60 days.
The RAP can be obtained free of cost from the following offices.
Government of Sikkim, Sikkim House, Panchsheel Marg, New Delhi
Customer service timings: 09:30 AM to 05:00 PM. ILP issuing time at Melli is from 8 AM to 8 PM every day.

Foreigners or travel agents fill the application form with name, nationality, passport number & validity date, entry date and exit date, then submit it to the permit office (form provided at the permit office).

Submit a copy of the valid passport, visa and a passport-size photo. The office verifies the traveller detail sheet, passport, visa stamp, seal and signature. Invalid documents make the application invalid.
On successful verification, the permit is issued with a unique reference number, valid for a duration of 30 days.
A copy of the duly filled application form / permit is submitted to the Foreigners Registration Office (FRO) for record and entry into the database.
On issue of the permit, the foreigner may stay for 30 days unless prior permission for an extension is obtained.
While exiting, the foreigner must present themselves at the FRO office to record their exit details.

PAP for a group of two or more foreign tourists can be obtained through recognised Travel Agents of Sikkim registered with the Tourism Department, as per the Sikkim Registration of Tourist Trade Rules, 2008.

Trekking permits in protected areas are issued free of cost by the Assistant Director, Sikkim Tourism Office, Gangtok. Trekkers must also provide a valid physical fitness certificate from a competent central / state government medical officer.

If a foreigner intends to visit a Protected / Restricted Area for activities other than tourism on a non-tourist visa, prior permission of the Ministry of Home Affairs must be taken before granting PAP / RAP.

PAP / RAP for a specific purpose (business, employment, studies, etc.) is endorsed on the passport. For areas not open for tourism on a tourist visa, prior reference is made to the Ministry of Home Affairs.
A foreigner holding a non-tourist visa but visiting only for tourism may be granted a Special Permit for places that are open for tourism.
Citizens of Nepal and Bangladesh may produce a valid identity card reflecting their origin. All foreign visitors must register within 24 hours of arrival, and the permit is issued free of cost.

paragraphs: The three ethnic communities — Lepcha, Bhutia and Nepali — give Sikkim its folk dances and songs, an ingrained part of the state’s culture. This music relates to the beauty of the natural surroundings, depicts the harvest season, and is performed for good luck and prosperity.

This group dance of the Tamang community, with robust foot tapping and the elaborate sound and display of the Damphu instrument, is performed on all happy occasions and highlights the vigour and vitality of the community. Tamang songs known as “Hwai” are full of human emotions — so popular that no Nepali merrymaking is considered complete without singing one.
Through this romantic group dance, performed by a group of male and female dancers, the joys of life and feelings of happiness are shared during the harvesting season and on other happy occasions.

The literal meaning of “Chu” is Snowy Range, while “Faat” means Worship. This group folk dance is performed in honour of Mount Khangchendzonga, the guardian deity of the Sikkimese people. The dancers, carrying butter lamps and green bamboo leaves, perform a ritualistic dance while singing devotional songs.

This group dance, comprising boys and girls, is performed to pay homage to past saints such as Guru Rimpoche and present saints in order to receive their blessings. The musical instruments that support the graceful steps of the dancers are Flute, Yangjey, Drum and Yarka.

Kagyed means the oral transmission of the eight Tantric Gods found in Tantric Buddhism — “Ka” means oral transmission, “Gyed” means eight and “Chham” means ritualistic dance. Held every year in various Sikkimese monasteries, it is a time of celebration for the Bhutias as they welcome the New Year, visiting monasteries and offering prayers by lighting butter lamps and offering cash and kind.

In this beautiful group dance of the Damai community, nine kinds of musical instruments are used to perfection — two types of Senai (Shehnai), Turhi (small and big), Damaha (Nagara) of two types, Tuyamko (small Dhol) of two types, Dholki and Jhyamta (cymbal). The Naumati Baja is a regular feature during weddings and other auspicious occasions.

A group of boys and girls, through this dance, try to invoke benign deities to shower fortunes on their home. They also remember some animal deities to bring good fortune and prosperity to the people. It is also performed during the consecration of a new house and to bless a newly married couple.

Based on a famous Lepcha folklore often retold to new generations as lyrical poetry. According to the legend, this group dance is performed to save people from the onslaught of mighty mountainous rivers. The Lepchas living on Tendong Hill in South Sikkim offered prayers to God through this dance, desiring to be saved from the rising water. As per folklore, God came as a bird and began sprinkling sacred millet beer on the water; soon the level subsided and the people heaved a sigh of relief.

Depicts the movements of the yak and the simple lifestyle of mountain herdsmen. Dancers wear the costume and mask of the yak. The Chhams performed at Pemayangtse, Rumtek and Enchey are especially impressive and draw large audiences.

A famous Lepcha dance depicting the sowing, reaping and harvesting of paddy. Old and young join hands to sing and make merry, their graceful movements set against the pleasant sounds of seasonal birds.

Chyap-Brung is the traditional musical instrument of the Limboo community. It is like a Dholak in shape but much bigger in size. During the course of group dance, male dancers hang the instrument around their necks with the help of a rope and beat the drum with an open palm on one side and a stick on the other. Such a manoeuvre produces two different sounds which echo boldly in valleys and mountains.

paragraphs: A delicious blend of Tibetan, Nepali and Lepcha cooking — rooted in rice, foraged vegetables and fresh organic produce, prepared simply to let natural flavours shine.

The traditional food of Sikkim, known as Sikkimese cuisine, is a delicious blend of Tibetan, Nepali and Lepcha dishes drawn from the state’s many ethnic tribes and communities. It is largely based on rice, with culinary vegetables foraged from the jungle and a generous use of fresh and fermented produce.

Most Sikkimese people are meat eaters, and a variety of fresh and processed meats feature in almost every meal. Dishes are generally stir-fried, boiled or steamed, with very limited use of spices and herbs — letting the fresh, organic ingredients shine.

A mildly sweet, ring-shaped rice bread — an addictive Nepali snack traditionally made during Tihar. The rice batter is enriched with a few spices and ghee, then poured by hand into hot oil and deep-fried until golden brown and crispy. It is often enjoyed with a meat-based curry.
A Tibetan deep-fried bread stuffed with a spiced minced-chicken filling and crimped into a pretty edge — crispy outside, juicy inside. Served hot with your favourite sauce or chutney.
A wholesome and nourishing traditional nettle soup — simple, tangy and warming, made from sisnu (nettle) with a hint of garlic and lemon.

A traditional cheese made from buttermilk. The boiled solids are drained in cloth to form a soft, ricotta-like cheese, often fermented for a tangy taste. For the hard variety it is pressed, dried, cubed and hung over fire to harden further.
Steamed dumplings filled with meat or vegetables — a beloved Himalayan favourite served hot with fiery chilli sauce.

3Roll into ~3.5-inch circles. Place filling on one, top with another, and pinch the edges firmly, then crimp all around.
4Deep-fry on medium heat until golden brown on both sides. Serve hot with sauce or chutney.

3Let it cool slightly, then stir in a teaspoon of lemon juice.

2Wrap and hang it in a thin cloth to drain; let it ferment slightly for a tangy taste.

2Mix flour and salt with a little water into a stiff dough; divide into balls and roll into thin circles.
3Place the filling in the centre, then fold and pleat the edges into shape.
4Steam for 15–20 minutes and serve hot with chilli sauce (the water makes a good soup).

paragraphs: From sub-tropical valleys in the south to snow-bound tundra in the north, Sikkim packs an astonishing range of climates into a small Himalayan canvas.

Sikkim’s geographical location and dramatic altitudinal variation give it tropical, temperate and alpine climates within an area of just 7,096 sq. km. Temperatures range from sub-tropical in the southern lower parts to cold deserts in the snowy north.

It is also the most humid region in the entire Himalayan range, owing to its proximity to the Bay of Bengal and direct exposure to the southern monsoon. Most inhabited regions enjoy a temperate climate, with temperatures seldom exceeding 28 °C in summer and an average annual temperature of around 18 °C.
Sikkim enjoys pleasant weather year-round, and a trip can be planned anytime depending on your interests. That said, every season offers something distinct — and two windows stand out.
Blooming natural beauty across Gangtok — colourful flora at its peak.
Crisp, clear views of the Himalayan range — perfect for photography.

Sikkim has two rainy seasons — summer rains and winter rains. The southern part sees more summer rain, while the north receives winter rain during August and September. Rainfall is heavy and well distributed from May to early October, decreasing from south to north.
Tip: explore the north during May and June, and the south during August and September — mindful of occasional blocked roads and delayed flights.

Lying in the lap of the Himalayas, Sikkim is one of the few states in India to receive regular snowfall. The tundra-type north stays snowbound for four months a year, with night-time temperatures routinely dropping below freezing.
items: Snow blankets most areas — a charming snowy getaway.
Festivals: Losoong, Losar, Maghey Sankranti & Gutor Cham.
Bearably cold days, sub-zero nights — pack warm.
Pleasant, moderate weather — ideal for sightseeing.
Blooming rhododendrons & orchids; the Flower Festival.
Trekking, rafting, kayaking, mountain biking & more.
Lush, rejuvenated landscapes & roaring waterfalls.
A chirpy heaven for bird watchers — spot rare species.
Fewer tourists — cheaper accommodation.
July is the wettest month in most places.
Highest annual rainfall may exceed 5,000 mm.
Rainy days range from 100 (Thangu) to 184 (Gangtok).
Two seasons: summer rain in the south, winter rain in the north.
Kanchenjunga temperatures can drop to -32 °C.

High north-western peaks can fall to -40 °C in winter.
Snow lingers till the end of March in most places.
